name: Julian Goodare
specialization: Scottish witchcraft prosecutions; digital database methodology; state anxiety and persecution

major_works.title: The Survey of Scottish Witchcraft (online database)
major_works.significance: Comprehensive digital database of all known Scottish witchcraft cases; foundational resource for quantitative Scottish witchcraft research

major_works.title: The Scottish Witch-Hunt in Context (editor)
major_works.significance: Edited volume contextualizing Scottish cases within European framework; includes multiple methodological approaches

major_works.title: State and Society in Early Modern Scotland
major_works.significance: Broader political history framework within which the witchcraft study is embedded

core_argument: Scottish witch-hunting was driven by state and elite anxiety about social order, particularly during periods of political and religious instability. The prosecution pattern correlates with moments of heightened state concern about disorder rather than with grassroots community accusations. Goodare builds on Larner but emphasizes state mechanisms over popular pressure.

methodological_approach.primary_materials: Complete surviving Scottish witchcraft case records systematically surveyed in the Survey of Scottish Witchcraft database; privy council, circuit court, and presbytery records
methodological_approach.analysis_target: Temporal and geographic patterns of prosecution; social characteristics of accused; institutional mechanisms of prosecution
methodological_approach.evidence_type: Digital database analysis; quantitative pattern identification across full surviving record set
methodological_approach.explanatory_level: State institutional and political: elite anxiety and institutional capacity driving prosecution

key_contributions.claim: Complete systematic survey of ~4,000 named accused persons in Scotland enables quantitative analysis of patterns impossible from case studies
key_contributions.implication: Digital humanities methodology can transform witchcraft historiography by providing population-level data

key_contributions.claim: Prosecution peaks correlate with specific moments of political crisis and state anxiety rather than with continuous popular demand
key_contributions.implication: The timing of prosecutions is explained by state dynamics, not by fluctuating popular belief

key_contributions.claim: Prosecution intensity reflects the availability of institutional machinery (willing magistrates, accessible courts, Kirk pressure) as much as the degree of witch belief
key_contributions.implication: Institutional history must be integrated with intellectual and social history

reception_and_critique.major_influences: Christina Larner, Scottish institutional history, digital humanities methodology
criticisms: State-anxiety model may overweight top-down factors relative to community-level dynamics
Database-driven approach can obscure local narrative texture that case studies reveal
Scotland remains a special case; applicability of conclusions to other regions contested

historiographical_significance: Goodare's Survey of Scottish Witchcraft database is the model for digital humanities approaches to witchcraft prosecution records and has made Scottish witchcraft data the most comprehensively documented in Europe. His theoretical emphasis on state anxiety updated and extended Larner's framework with new methodological tools. His work is central to current quantitative approaches to European witch-hunting.
source_method: Published scholarship and critical historiographical reconstruction
